## RADIO SPECTRUM POLICY GROUP

## Opinion

## on

## 6G spectrum roadmap

RSPG Opinion on a 6G spectrum roadmap

1 Background and scope of work The European Commission published in February 2024 the White Paper on “How to master Europe's digital infrastructure needs?”, to which the RSPG provided its Opinion. The RSPG noted that the focus should be kept on making radio spectrum available in due time to meet future needs in the EU and promote European competitiveness. The RSPG underlined that any future plans for the rollout of 6G in the EU need to take into account coverage and capacity demands, competition aspects and align to national demands and specificities such as the geographic and demographic landscape. The 5G spectrum roadmap developed by the RSPG in 2016 was widely welcomed by both Member States (MS) and stakeholders, underscoring the critical importance of establishing a clear roadmap ahead of launching a new generation of mobile networks. In accordance with the RSPG Work Programme for 2024-2025, the Group, after completing the first deliverable on 6G i.e., the RSPG Report on 6G Strategic vision, has now focused on the development of a 6G spectrum roadmap for the EU. The global vision and timeline for 6G development is set by the ITU-R, and currently the work on IMT-2030 is in the phase of definition of relevant requirements (2024-2026). This provides the RSPG with a valuable opportunity to deliver an EU-level 6G spectrum roadmap ahead of the next standards development phase, noting spectrum identified at WRC-23 and the possible additional spectrum identification at the upcoming WRC in 2027, if incumbent services can be protected. The target for technology development, including providing the necessary harmonised spectrum, is to enable the launch of 6G networks by 2030, with broader implementation continuing in the years that follow. This timeline should also be supported by EU spectrum policy to enable the initial launch of 6G networks and services across the EU. The RSPG Report on 6G Strategic vision addresses issues beyond the mere identification of possible spectrum bands for the initial 6G rollout, including for example interworking with non-terrestrial networks, spectrum sharing solutions, and authorisation regimes in 6G. Further assessment of these issues might facilitate the establishment of the 6G ecosystem and the 6G rollout in Europe. This opinion takes into account recent RSPG reports and opinions 1:

2 Public consultation 
A public consultation on the draft version of this RSPG opinion was held between 
13 February and 27 March 2026. All non-confidential responses are published on the 
RSPG website 2. The RSPG appreciated all comments received. The RSPG considered them 
carefully and improved the draft opinion as appropriate. The list of the stakeholders that 
responded to the public consultation can be found in Annex I. 

The RSPG welcomes the number of responses received from a diverse range of stakeholders representing the majority of the parties with an interest in the development of 6G networks or incumbents with an interest in the future spectrum policy. The wide support for this Opinion from stakeholders was clear. As expected, some of the individual comments reflect self-interest and as a consequence opposite views on the same topic are presented by different parties.

3 The opinion of the RSPG on the strategic spectrum roadmap towards 6G for 
Europe 
Expecting the availability of 6G systems by 2030, this spectrum roadmap has been 
developed to facilitate the launch of 6G on a large scale in Europe. The goal is to create 
a common ecosystem and market for network and terminal equipment in Europe so that 
the benefits of 6G services are available to all European citizens in a timely manner, 
driving industrial and societal transformation and economic growth in Europe from 
2030 and beyond. In its recent 6G strategic vision, RSPG recalled that coordinated 
timing for a launch of 6G services does not appear practical at EU level in the current 
harmonised bands due to technology neutrality and operators' migration plans for 
switching to enhanced technologies and that additional spectrum band(s) in EU could 
facilitate coordinated timing for 6G launch. This opinion identifies the frequency 
band(s) that should be made available for the launch of 6G mass market and for 
supporting development of various vertical markets and responding to relevant market 
demand and various European and national 6G policies. 
1. The RSPG is of the opinion that 6G can be implemented in all frequency bands 
already harmonised for ECS (WBB): 
• Low bands below 1 GHz: 700 MHz 3, 800 MHz 4, 900 MHz 5, in order to enable nationwide and indoor 6G coverage. 
• Mid bands: 1500 MHz 6, 1800 MHz 7, 2 GHz 8, 2.6 GHz 9, 3.6 GHz 10, in order to possibly support and supplement the roll-out of high capacity 6G networks in suburban and urban areas. 
• High bands: 26 GHz 11, 42 GHz 12, in order to enable very high-capacity hot spot 6G coverage. 2. The RSPG is of the opinion that the upper 6 GHz band will be the primary band suitable for the introduction of 6G in Europe by 2030. This band can enable implementation of 6G use cases that require more capacity than 5G services. According to the RSPG Opinion on the long-term vision for the upper 6 GHz band, the frequency range for 6G in this band depends on the outcome of the WRC-27 but consists of at least 540 MHz of continuous spectrum. This can contribute to fulfil the mobile industry and operators’ demands of additional contiguous 200 MHz of mid band spectrum per operator, enhancing coverage and capacity in suburban and urban areas while supporting the use of existing infrastructure and base station sites.

3. The RSPG notes that the 7125-7250 MHz band is under study in Region 1 at WRC-27 for possible identification to IMT 13, and, if decided so, it could provide additional 6G spectrum complementing the upper 6 GHz band. The RSPG recommends that consideration should be given to the protection of incumbent services, and to feasible coexistence conditions to be defined at WRC-27 and further addressed in CEPT. 
4. The RSPG notes that the 6425-7125 MHz band is currently subject to an EC mandate 14 for future harmonised conditions in Europe taking into account the protection of incumbent services in this band and adjacent bands. In this regard, it is noted in the EC Mandate that the rollout of 6G should continue to facilitate the operation and evolution of relevant incumbent services in this band where required. The response to the EC mandate is expected to be completed by 2027. This timing is consistent with a 6G launch in 2030. The RSPG encourages consumer equipment manufacturers to treat the 6425-7250 MHz range as one consistent block of spectrum regardless of the range finally harmonised for ECS (WBB) in Europe, in order to avoid market fragmentation. 
5. The RSPG recommends that CEPT reviews the technical and regulatory conditions for all frequency bands harmonised under the Radio Spectrum Decision for mobile networks in order to ensure that they are suitable for 6G. 
6. The RSPG recognises that most frequency bands harmonised for (WBB) ECS are already in use across Europe by previous ECS generations. To facilitate the introduction of 6G, the RSPG recommends that: 
• Mobile equipment manufacturers develop network and terminal equipment that support 6G technology within these frequency bands. 
• Mobile network operators plan the migration of existing networks to 6G in line with their market strategies, needs, and the availability of relevant equipment. 7. The RSPG notes that the high bands (26 GHz and 42 GHz) offering very high capacity were harmonised for (WBB) ECS already in 2019 and 2024 respectively but remain widely unused by (WBB) ECS up to now. The RSPG further notes that these bands cannot replace mid-band spectrum as a capacity band for wider area 6G. However, the RSPG encourages mobile equipment manufacturers to accelerate the development of devices supporting these bands and invites both mobile network operators and private network operators to actively utilise these frequencies. 8. The RSPG is of the opinion that the 3.8-4.2 GHz band, harmonised with Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/2425 15 , is suitable for developing low/medium power local area networks also using 6G technology to support the growth of various vertical markets. The RSPG notes that other frequency bands are also being made available for local networks on a national level by Member States, and that these frequency bands could likewise be suitable for local 6G networks.
